“I might equally ask,” she answered, “why, with such a plain intention of insulting and offending me, you thought fit to declare that you liked me against your inclination, against your reason, and even against your character. Did not that furnish some excuse for incivility, if I was indeed uncivil? Yet I have other provocations, as you well know. Had my feelings not already determined against you, had I been indifferent, or even favourably disposed, can you imagine that any consideration could persuade me to accept the man who has destroyed, perhaps beyond repair, the happiness of a sister so dearly beloved?”

Mr. Darcy's colour altered as she spoke, but the disturbance was brief, and he heard her without any effort to interrupt as she proceeded:

“I have every possible cause to think ill of you. No intention can excuse the unjust and ungenerous role you played in that affair. You dare not deny, you cannot deny, that you were the chief, if not the sole instrument in separating them, leaving one exposed to the world's blame for fickleness and uncertainty, the other to its mockery for hopes disappointed, and plunging both into the keenest misery.”

She stopped, and observed with considerable indignation that his manner of listening betrayed not the least remorse. He even regarded her with a smile of pretended disbelief.

“Can you deny having done this?” she asked again.

Then, with an assumed composure, he replied, “I have no desire to deny that I used every means in my power to part my friend from your sister, nor that I rejoice at having succeeded. To him I have shown greater kindness than to myself.”

Elizabeth scorned to appear to notice this civil remark, though she understood it perfectly, and it was little calculated to soften her resentment.

“But this business alone,” she continued, “does not account for my dislike. My judgment of you was formed long before it occurred. Your character was disclosed by the narrative Mr. Wickham gave me many months since. What can you offer upon that subject? By what fancied act of friendship will you defend yourself there? Or by what misrepresentation will you contrive to deceive others?”

“You show an eager concern for that gentleman's affairs,” Darcy said, less calmly and with a deepening colour.

“Who can learn what his misfortunes have been without feeling concerned for him?”

“His misfortunes!” Darcy repeated with contempt. “Yes, his misfortunes have been exceedingly great.”

“And you inflicted them,” Elizabeth cried with spirit. “You have brought him to his present poverty—comparative poverty.

Winters near Sullivan's Island are rarely very harsh, and in autumn people almost never think a fire necessary. Around the middle of October, 18—, however, there was an unusually cold day. Just before sunset I struggled through the evergreen bushes to my friend's hut. I had not visited for several weeks. At the time I lived in Charleston, nine miles from the island, and traveling back and forth was much harder than it is today. I knocked as usual, but nobody answered. Knowing where the key was hidden, I fetched it, unlocked the door, and went inside. A fine fire burned on the hearth. This was something new, and very welcome. I took off my overcoat, settled into an armchair beside the crackling logs, and waited patiently for my hosts to return.

They arrived soon after dark and greeted me warmly. Jupiter, grinning broadly, busied himself preparing marsh hens for supper. Legrand was in one of his bursts of enthusiasm—I do not know what else to call them. He had found an unknown shellfish with a two-part shell, belonging to an entirely new genus. Better still, with Jupiter's help he had tracked down and caught a scarab beetle that he believed was completely new. He wanted my opinion on it the next morning.

“Why not tonight?” I asked, warming my hands over the flames and wishing the whole tribe of scarab beetles to the devil.

“If only I'd known you were here!” Legrand said. “But I haven't seen you for so long. How could I have guessed you'd choose this particular evening to visit? Coming home, I met Lieutenant G—— from the fort, and foolishly lent him the insect. So you can't possibly see it before morning. Stay here tonight, and I'll send Jup to fetch it at sunrise. It's the most beautiful thing in creation!”

“What is—sunrise?”

“Of course not! The beetle. It's a brilliant gold, about the size of a large hickory nut. There are two jet-black spots near one end of its back and a somewhat longer one at the other end. Its antennae are—”

“There isn't any tin in it, Master Will, as I keep telling you,” Jupiter interrupted. “That bug is gold, solid gold, every bit of it, inside too, except the wings. I've never held a bug even half as heavy in my life.”

“Absolutely delightful!” Mrs. Clay exclaimed, though she did not dare glance at Anne. “Just like a father and son! Dear Miss Elliot, may I call them father and son?”

“Oh, I don't place restrictions on anyone's words. If you insist on having such ideas! But honestly, I hardly notice his attentions being any greater than other men's.”

“My dear Miss Elliot!” cried Mrs. Clay, raising her hands and eyes, then conveniently allowing silence to express the rest of her amazement.

“Well, my dear Penelope, you needn't worry so much about him. I did invite him, you know. I sent him away smiling. When I learned that he really was spending the whole of tomorrow with his friends at Thornberry Park, I took pity on him.”

Anne admired the friend's skill as an actress. She could display such pleasure both at the prospect and at the actual arrival of the very man whose presence must obstruct her chief ambition. Mrs. Clay could hardly fail to hate the sight of Mr. Elliot. Yet she managed to look entirely obliging and serene, apparently content with having her freedom restricted and being able to devote only half as much attention to Sir Walter as she otherwise would.

For Anne herself, seeing Mr. Elliot enter was deeply distressing, and having him come over and speak to her was positively painful. Previously she had sometimes felt he could not be entirely sincere; now she detected insincerity in everything. His respectful attentiveness to her father, set against his earlier words, was repulsive. Remembering his cruelty towards Mrs. Smith, she could scarcely endure his present smiles and gentleness or listen to his artificially noble sentiments.

She intended to avoid any change in behavior sharp enough to make him challenge her about it. Escaping questions or a scene mattered greatly to her. Still, she meant to be as firmly cool as their family relationship allowed and to withdraw as quietly as possible from the few unnecessary steps towards intimacy she had gradually been persuaded to take. Accordingly, she was more reserved and distant than she had been the previous evening.

He tried to revive her curiosity about how and where he had once heard her praised, very much wanting the pleasure of having her beg for further information. But the spell was broken. He discovered that the warmth and excitement of a public gathering were needed to stir his modest cousin's vanity. At least, he found he could not stir it now with any of the attempts he could risk while the others demanded so much of his attention.
